title: GPU Hydra slowdowns - nightshift ops notes and followups
content:
Summary:
Nightshift observed a series of brief (30s-4m) latency spikes across multiple dedicated GPU pools in us-west-2 between 02:10–06:20 local. Spikes were not correlated with a single tenant traffic burst; instead they presented as low-amplitude, high-frequency slowdowns affecting small proportions of concurrent requests (1–7% P95 elevation). We nicknamed the phenomenon 'Hydra' because spikes popped up on different hosts in quick succession and then resolved.

Immediate impact:
- Host pools: dedicated-pool-03, dedicated-pool-07 (NVIDIA-A100 equiv), and a few ephemerals in staging.
- Customer-facing: transient P95 increases; errors stayed low. Some high-SLA customers reported degraded tail latency during a 30-minute window.
- Autoscaler: several nodes were added/removed rapidly; observed hysteresis (flapping) leading to noisy scaling decisions.

What we saw (signals):
- Metrics: small, correlated P95 bumps across multiple pods/hosts. CPU on control-plane remained steady. GPU utilization dipped slightly during spikes (token throughput down).
- Node telemetry: short-lived thermal excursions on GPU sensors that did not exceed driver thresholds but coincided with driver-level throttling events (nvml throttle reason code 0x04).
- cgroups/containers: increased kernel scheduling latency, and occasional long syscalls from allocation hot loops during KV cache refill.
- Allocator: transient backpressure with queue depth spikes for tenant-specific queues.
- Logs: repeated device reset warnings on hosts showing later firmware-signature mismatch warnings in driver logs.
- Traces: requests that hit cold KV cache and triggered large kv-cache allocations were more likely to be in the slow cohort.

Initial mitigation (nightshift actions):
1) Temporarily increased autoscaler min-headroom for affected pools (+20%) to avoid reactive scale-in during noisy windows.
2) Drained and cycled two worst-affected hosts (dp-03-12 and dp-07-04) that showed repeat thermal throttle events and elevated driver warnings.
3) Enabled per-tenant soft-throttles on a handful of heavy tenants suspected of causing frequent KV-cache churn — quick rollback available.
4) Escalated to infra-oncall for firmware log review and requested host health dumps.

Hypotheses (ranked):
A) Thermal micro-throttles triggered by driver/firmware mismatch: sensors show brief temp/sensor anomalies that appear with driver-level partial throttling (nvml code). Firmware mismatch warning suggests some hosts on mixed firmware versions.
B) KV-cache amplification: certain long-context requests cause large KV cache loads and allocations that temporarily contend on GPU memory bandwidth and host PCIe, producing latency spikes.
C) Autoscaler hysteresis + aggressive scale-in: autoscaler shrink during low average usage leaves less headroom, so when Hydra happens the system overreacts and creates oscillation that amplifies visible tail latency.
D) A subtle noisy-tenant pattern: several smaller tenants intermittently do short bursts that align and multiply kernel contention across nodes.

Experiments run (nightshift + next 24h):
- Synthetic hammer: reproduced small KV-cache heavy workload in staging against mixed-firmware hosts; observed similar micro-throttles when background temp cycles induced by our stress test.
- Per-host isolate: moved a suspected noisy tenant to a single-host cage (anti-affinity) to observe cross-tenant coupling; correlation dropped for hosts with isolated tenant.
- Autoscaler sim: bumped scale-in cooldown and headroom in a canary pool; observed reduced flapping and lower P95 variance.

Immediate follow-ups (action items):
- SRE: Create a short-running automated detector for nvml throttle reason 0x04 bursts (owner: Marco) — timeline: 1 week.
- Infra: Audit GPU firmware across dedicated pools and schedule coordinated firmware homogenization for mixed-firmware hosts (owner: Ravi) — timeline: 2 weeks with rolling-safe reboots.
- Serving Runtime: Add KV-cache allocation histograms to tracing for long-context requests (owner: Janelle) — timeline: 2 sprints.
- Autoscaler: Add conservative default headroom for Dedicated pools and reduce scale-in aggression during nighttime windows (owner: eng-platform) — timeline: 1 sprint.
- Product/Trusted-Customers: Notify affected high-SLA customers with post-incident note and expected remediation plan (owner: Customer Success) — timeline: 3 business days.

Runbook draft snippets (to include in site-runbook/gpu-dedicated-playbook):
- Detection: if >3 hosts in a pool report nvml throttle reason 0x04 within 10m OR P95 increases >30% for >15m, flag as Hydra-like event.
- Immediate steps: (1) increase dedicated-pool headroom by +30% for the pool (2) mark suspected hosts with "soft isolation" label to avoid scheduling new heavy tenants (3) drain and cycle hosts that show driver reset or repeated nvml warnings.
- Tenant isolation checklist: identify top-3 tenants by recent allocation rate, move to anti-affinity cage, watch for correlation drop for 60m.
- Autoscaler safeguards: enforce min-replicas floor during detection and add a 10m scale-in cooldown.

Notes-to-self / informal observations:
- The driver warnings are subtle — they were buried in host journald with timestamps shifted by ~90s compared to application traces. Add a script to correlate host-journal timestamps with request traces.
- I think we under-instrument KV-cache churn paths; we have size metrics but not allocation-rate per-request. That's where most of the slow ones appear to cluster.
- Nightshift felt that the thermal spikes were likely exacerbated by nearby jobs (non-dedicated experiments) on the same racks; need rack-level placement awareness for Dedicated.

Open questions / unresolved:
- Are mixed firmware hosts truly the root cause, or just amplifying an already-present KV-cache allocation problem?
- How often are tenant bursts coinciding purely by chance vs. application-level coupling?
- Would more aggressive prewarming of KV caches for long-context tenants materially reduce Hydra occurrences?

Suggested follow-up experiment backlog (prioritized):
1) Full firmware homogenization pilot on 10 hosts + synthetic KV-cache workload run.
2) Add allocation-rate tracing and run correlation analysis with thermal events (30d window).
3) Autoscaler policy A/B test (current vs conservative-headroom) across 2 regions for 2 weeks.
4) Implement tenant anti-affinity as a defensive scheduling knob and test on canary tenants.

Communication log (short):
- 2024-04-22 02:34 — Slack #sre: "observing brief P95 spikes across dp-03 + dp-07; investigating" (Aisha)
- 2024-04-22 02:52 — PagerDuty triggered; nightshift responded and started mitigations (Marco)
- 2024-04-22 03:40 — Infra paged for firmware logs (Ravi)

Draft post-incident notes (to customer-success/ops):
- Root cause: multi-factor; likely interaction between KV-cache allocation patterns and intermittent driver-level thermal throttles on mixed-firmware hosts, amplified by autoscaler sensitivity.
- Short-term fix: increased pool headroom, drained/rebooted noisy hosts, tenant isolation.
- Medium-term: firmware homogenization, better KV-cache tracing, autoscaler policy adjustments.

TODO (short):
- [ ] Marco: detector alarm for nvml throttle bursts.
- [ ] Ravi: create firmware inventory + roll plan.
- [ ] Janelle: instrument allocation-rate per request.
- [ ] Eng-platform: deploy conservative headroom defaults and test.
- [ ] Aisha: draft customer-facing timeline and FAQ.

Appendix: useful queries and commands (for oncall)
- k get pods -l pool=dedicated-pool-03 -o wide (find suspect pods)
- nvmldiag show --host dp-03-12 --since 1h | grep -i throttle (collect throttle lines)
- trace-query "kv_cache_alloc_rate" | group_by(host, 5m) | top(20) (ad-hoc trace)

End of note. Still rough — will convert into a runbook page and a short postmortem once experiments finish.
